title: IO-bound vs Compute-bound: quantization probe (INT8/FP8/GPTQ/AWQ)
content:
Purpose:
This is a working note from a short lab sweep to determine when quantized workloads become IO-bound vs compute-bound. Focused vectors: INT8 (GEMM kernels), FP8 kernels (new compiler paths), GPTQ/AWQ kernels (permuted memory layouts), and the interaction with data movement (host->device memcpys, staging buffers, transpose).

Background and motivation:
We have several customer cases where switching to INT8 or AWQ reduces raw compute time but the observed latency improvement in production is less than expected. Hypothesis: for small batch shapes and short contexts, host/device transfer + in-host preprocessing (transpose/packing) and kernel launch jitter dominate. For larger batch shapes / long contexts, GPU compute becomes dominant and we see more straightforward improvements. We need concrete numbers and a reproducible microbench to inform the runtime's kernel selection and memory path optimizations (pinned memory, fused-transpose kernels, async prefetch).

Hypotheses:
- H1: For batch_size*seq_len < ~4k tokens on an A100/RTX GPU, the workload is IO-bound: memcpy+transpose overhead >= kernel execution.
- H2: AWQ/GPTQ layouts increase host-side packing cost; unless we use fused host-to-device packing, measured latency will regress vs a straightforward INT8 GEMM kernel for small seqs.
- H3: FP8 kernels reduce compute time but increase memory footprint transiently (wider activation path) leading to higher device memory churn and occasional paging/GC spikes on multi-tenant nodes.

Experimental setup (exact):
- Hardware: A100 40GB (single GPU), RTX 6000 Ada (single GPU) for comparison. Host: Ubuntu 22.04, 2x socket Intel Cascade Lake, 192GB RAM. PCIe gen3 topology for A100 runs (note: NVLINK not available for single-GPU).
- Models: 7B family (Llama 2 7B fp32 baseline), compiled into four variants: FP32 (baseline), FP8 (compiler path - newest kernels), INT8-GPTQ (per-layer quant), AWQ (per-channel, block-quant layout).
- Kernels: our runtime exposes kernel variants: gemm-direct-int8 (packed on-device), pack-then-gemm-awq (host packing + device kernel), fused-h2d-pack-gemm (experimental fused path), fp8-kernel-v2.
- Client traffic: synthetic single-request-per-connection generator reproducing PL short-chat mix: prompt tokens [8..64], completion target [16 tokens], temperature sampling disabled (deterministic), streaming disabled. 10k requests per profile run.
- Measurement: for each bench we capture P50/P95/P99 latency (end-to-end), kernel_time (device-side measured via CUPTI), host_prehandoff_time (time spent in runtime preparing contiguous buffers + transpose), h2d_bytes and h2d_time (measured via nvprof-like sampling), CPU utilization, GPU SM utilization, PCIe throughput traces (nvidia-smi dmon sampling 100ms).
- Warmups: 200 requests warmup. Each experiment repeated 3x and median selected.

Key commands (repro):
- runtime bench: ./bench_driver --model <variant> --batch 1 --seq 32 --count 10000 --profile cups
- debug logging: RUNTIME_DEBUG=memcopy,pack,launch ./runtime ...

Results (summary):
- Small shapes (batch=1, seq=16-32): host_prehandoff_time dominated (40-60% of latency) for AWQ/GPTQ kernels. Measurements show host-pack for AWQ takes ~120-220 us per request (depends on blocksize / channel counts). GPU kernel execution for INT8: ~80-110 us; AWQ device kernel ~60 us but host packing pushes total higher. FP8 kernel execution ~45-70 us.
- Medium shapes (batch=2..4, seq=64): kernel execution becomes ~60-80% of overall latency; compute wins and FP8/INT8 show clear improvement vs FP32.
- Long shapes (seq 512+ streaming tokens): compute clearly dominant; quantization wins are proportional to token compute.
- P95/P99 tails: AWQ/GPTQ exhibit heavier tails at small shapes due to host-side GC/alloc jitter when using non-pinned staging buffers. Switching to pinned buffers + reuse reduces tail by ~30%.
- PCIe saturation: when batching multiple concurrent small requests (multi-tenant simulation, 8 parallel clients), aggregate h2d bandwidth approaches 60-70% of PCIe bandwidth and booking/queueing on host threads increases latency variance.

Representative microprofile snippet (tokens=32):
- INT8 (gemm-direct-int8): end2end P50=220us, host_prehandoff=70us, h2d_time=25us, kernel=90us, tail P95=430us
- AWQ (pack-host + kernel): end2end P50=310us, host_prehandoff=180us, h2d_time=30us, kernel=60us, tail P95=760us
- FP8-v2 (fused path): end2end P50=200us, host_prehandoff=35us, h2d_time=20us, kernel=120us, tail P95=360us

Observations and interpretations:
- AWQ's host packing cost is the primary culprit for small-shape regressions. The device kernel is lean but suffers because we are doing expensive memory layout transformations on CPU and then memcpy.
- Using pinned memory and reusing staging buffers dramatically reduces h2d_time and tail. Allocating pinned buffers up front is net-positive even though pinned allocations are a limited resource.
- Fusing pack into H2D (doing packing kernel on device after an async host copy of raw contiguous tokens) is promising: it moves CPU work to GPU and reduces host-side latency, but it increases device kernel complexity and requires careful overlapping to avoid additional device-to-device copies.
- FP8 kernels reduce compute time but they increase peak scratch memory in our implementation; on nodes with high tenant density we see occasional OOM-like spikes or transient memory pressure.
- Multi-client concurrent small requests expose host scheduler/lock contention (mutexes around allocator and per-stream queues). We observed that per-thread staging buffer pools + lock-free queues reduce contention.

Quick mitigations validated during sweep:
- Preallocate pinned staging buffers per serving thread (size tuned to max seq); reuse across requests. Reduced tail latency ~30% on AWQ small shapes.
- Introduce small request fast-path: if seq*batch < threshold and kernel supports on-device packing, route to fused-h2d-pack-gemm; falls back to host pack only if device fused path unavailable.
- Per-request profiling flag that emits prehand-off time and h2d time into traces so we can build per-route heuristics in the console.

Recommendations for runtime roadmap (short/mid term):
- Short (2w): Implement pinned buffer pool + per-thread allocator; enable by default for small shapes and AWQ/GPTQ kernels.
- Short (3w): Add per-route quant probe metrics (host_pack_time, h2d_time, device_kernel_time) to the Console so customers can see when their workloads are IO vs compute bound.
- Mid (6w): Finish fused-h2d-pack-gemm path and add kernel selection policy: choose fused device-pack when host_pack_cost > expected kernel gain.
- Mid (8-12w): Add automatic pinned buffer sizing and eviction heuristics for multi-tenant hosts (avoid pinned leakage).

Open questions / next experiments:
- Measure NVLINK vs PCIe difference (multi-GPU and multi-instance) — hypothesis: NVLINK mitigates h2d pressure when KV cache is remote.
- Validate fused-pack approach at scale with long sequences and multi-batch convergence; check memory amplification.
- Investigate further FP8 scratch memory patterns: can we compress intermediate scratch or spill to device-level cache to avoid OOM spikes?
- Microbenchmark other packaging strategies: SIMD host pack (AVX512) vs GPU pack — quantify crossovers.
